intro: Projects you could start this week, each tied to the deals that make it timely. Every idea lists open datasets with links, a first milestone you can hit in about two weeks, and what you need to run it. Refreshed with the twice-daily deals brief.
since_last_run: No changes to the ideas this run. No new qualifying deals landed, so the seven active ideas, their evidence and datasets stand; none of them cited the two Sep 23 deals that aged out of the brief.

ideas.title: Does more perturbation data actually help? A scaling test for virtual-cell models
ideas.question: As training data grows from thousands to millions of perturbed cells, do perturbation-response models beat a simple mean-shift baseline on genes and cell lines they have not seen, and where does the curve flatten?
ideas.why_now: Big tech and pharma are paying for perturbation data at scale: Google DeepMind, Isomorphic and Meta put $300M into Biohub's open virtual-cell coalition, GSK, Pfizer and Sanofi joined Parse and Nomic's 100M-cell Cascade dataset, and Flagship rebuilt Etcelera around a 150M-cell model. Several published evaluations have found that simple baselines are hard to beat, so a clean scaling curve on open data would tell everyone whether the money is buying accuracy. Arc's 2026 Virtual Cell Challenge (zero-shot prediction in unseen cell lines) closed on Nov 5 and names winners in mid-to-late November, which gives you fresh methods to compare against.

datasets.name: Tahoe-100M
datasets.what: About 100M single cells from cancer cell lines treated with small molecules; drug perturbation atlas from Vevo (now Tahoe) and Arc

datasets.name: Replogle 2022 genome-wide Perturb-seq (via pertpy)
datasets.what: Genome-scale CRISPRi Perturb-seq in K562 (plus an RPE1 essential-gene screen), loadable in one line from pertpy

datasets.name: Arc Virtual Cell Atlas
datasets.what: Arc's collection of public perturbation data, including the full 2025 Virtual Cell Challenge dataset

approach: Fix the evaluation first: hold out whole perturbations and, separately, a whole cell line; score with differential-expression overlap and correlation of predicted vs. observed shifts on the top changed genes.
Build two baselines: the mean perturbation effect, and a linear model on gene embeddings (e.g. from gene co-expression).
Train one mid-size learned model (a fine-tuned single-cell foundation model or a published perturbation model) at 1%, 3%, 10%, 30% and 100% of the training cells and perturbations.
Plot accuracy against data size for each split, and compare where the curves cross the baselines.
ideas.first_milestone: Two weeks: reproduce the mean-baseline result on Replogle K562 with your evaluation code, and write down the gap a learned model has to close.
ideas.compute: One 24–48 GB GPU is enough for the Replogle work; stream or subset Tahoe rather than downloading all of it.
ideas.who_cares: Biohub and its partners, the Cascade pharma members, Etcelera, and every startup selling a proprietary atlas. A clear scaling answer tells them whether more cells or better models is the bottleneck.
ideas.risks: Metrics in this field are disputed; publish the evaluation code and report several metrics so the result is not an artifact of one score.

ideas.title: Can AI read preclinical tox slides? An open rat liver and kidney benchmark
ideas.question: Do pathology foundation models trained mostly on human tissue transfer to rat tox studies, and can they flag findings for compounds they have never seen?
ideas.why_now: AstraZeneca signed Tremont AI to speed up preclinical toxicology-pathology reads, a step that sits right before every IND. There is no widely used open benchmark for this, but Japan's Open TG-GATEs project released more than 53,000 rat liver and kidney slides covering 160 compounds, with recorded findings.

datasets.name: Open TG-GATEs Pathological Image Database
datasets.what: More than 53,000 whole-slide images of rat liver and kidney from 160 compounds, viewable alongside the recorded pathology findings
datasets.size: Large; start with one organ and a few dozen compounds

datasets.name: Open TG-GATEs (main database)
datasets.what: The paper describing the matching gene expression, dose and time-course data, so morphology can be linked to transcriptomics

approach: Pick liver, a handful of common findings (e.g. necrosis, hypertrophy, vacuolation) and a compound split where test compounds never appear in training.
Tile slides and extract features with two or three open pathology foundation models, plus an ImageNet model as a control.
Train attention-based multiple-instance learning per finding; report AUROC on held-out compounds and dose levels.
Stretch: predict the matching gene expression signature from the slide, or vice versa.
ideas.first_milestone: Two weeks: download 200 liver slides from 10 compounds, tile them, and get a first feature-plus-MIL baseline for one finding.
ideas.compute: Feature extraction is the heavy step: one GPU, several days, with a few TB of scratch disk.
ideas.who_cares: AstraZeneca and Tremont AI, CROs that run GLP tox studies, and AI drug developers moving assets into the clinic (Formation Bio, Biossil).
ideas.risks: Findings were recorded by different pathologists over many years; check label consistency on a sample before trusting the numbers.

ideas.title: How many placebo patients can a digital twin replace? A test on past ALS trials
ideas.area: Clinical trial AI / synthetic control arms
ideas.question: If you train a disease-progression model on placebo arms from older ALS trials, how much does adjusting for its predictions shrink the sample size a new trial needs, without biasing the treatment effect?
ideas.why_now: Trial-stage AI is drawing money and partners: Boehringer is testing Microsoft's digital patient twins and synthetic control arms, AstraZeneca and Oracle are working on AI-driven recruitment, Atlas Bio raised a $10M seed to simulate Phase II trials, and Formation Bio raised $600M to run drugs through an AI-native development platform. The open question for all of them is how many patients a model can stand in for, measured on real trials.

datasets.name: PRO-ACT (Pooled Resource Open-Access ALS Clinical Trials)
datasets.what: Pooled patient-level data from many completed ALS trials: ALSFRS-R scores over time, vitals, labs, demographics and treatment arm
datasets.access: Free with registration and a data-use agreement

datasets.name: Project Data Sphere
datasets.what: Shared patient-level oncology trial data, mostly comparator arms, for repeating the analysis in cancer

approach: Split by trial, not by patient: train on placebo arms from some trials and test on placebo arms from trials the model never saw.
Predict each patient's ALSFRS-R slope from baseline data with a few model types (mixed effects, gradient boosting, a small sequence model).
Use the prediction as a prognostic covariate in the primary analysis (the PROCOVA-style approach) and compute the variance reduction, which translates into equivalent patients saved.
Check type I error by re-running on placebo-vs-placebo comparisons.
ideas.first_milestone: Two weeks: get PRO-ACT access, rebuild a standard ALSFRS-R slope model, and report its error on one held-out trial.
ideas.who_cares: Microsoft and Boehringer, AstraZeneca, Atlas Bio, Formation Bio, and rare-disease sponsors who struggle to recruit placebo patients.
ideas.risks: Older trials used different inclusion rules than current ones; report how performance changes with trial era.

ideas.title: Do in-silico confidence scores predict which designed binders actually bind?
ideas.question: Across hundreds of community-designed binders that were tested in a lab, which computed scores (interface confidence, pLDDT, energy terms, sequence novelty) predict binding and expression, and how much do they add over each other?
ideas.why_now: Pharma is now licensing design models as standard tools: Roche and GSK signed Chai, UCB signed Cradle, Astellas licensed AI Proteins' miniproteins, and BigHat raised $75M for design plus wet-lab testing. All of them pick which designs to make using model confidence scores. Adaptyv Bio's open EGFR binder competitions released designs with lab measurements, and Cradle won one of the rounds, so the data comes from the same kind of tools these deals pay for.

datasets.name: Adaptyv EGFR binder competition, round 2
datasets.what: Designed EGFR binders with lab binding results, sequence-similarity checks and links to predicted structures

datasets.name: Adaptyv EGFR binder competition, round 1
datasets.what: The first round of the same competition, a second independent test set if its lab results line up with round 2

datasets.name: Crowdsourced Protein Design: lessons from the Adaptyv EGFR competition
datasets.what: The organisers' write-up, useful for understanding how the designs were selected and measured

approach: Assemble one table per round: sequence, design method, binding call or KD, expression.
Recompute a consistent set of scores for every design with one or two open structure predictors, so the scores are comparable across teams.
Measure how well each score ranks binders (AUROC, precision in the top 10%), then fit a simple combined model and test it from round 1 to round 2.
Report which scores carry real signal and which are redundant.
ideas.first_milestone: Two weeks: a clean merged table for round 2 with the competition's own metrics, and a first AUROC per metric.
ideas.compute: One GPU for re-running structure prediction on a few hundred complexes.
ideas.who_cares: Chai, Cradle, Generate, AI Proteins, BigHat and their pharma partners, all of whom choose what to synthesise from these scores.
ideas.risks: One target (EGFR) may not generalise; say so, and add other public design-plus-assay sets if you find them.

ideas.title: A self-driving loop on a benchtop robot: what works when you can only run 96 samples a round?
ideas.question: Which active-learning strategies reach a target fastest when each round is small (8–96 samples) and noisy, and can a $10K-class liquid handler run the loop on its own?
ideas.why_now: Money is flowing to the make-and-test layer: Opentrons raised a $40M Series E for AI-driven benchtop robots, Warp launched with $215M for automated chemistry, Multiply Labs raised $75M for robotic manufacturing, Danaher is building NVIDIA AI into its instruments, and Xaira introduced X-Automate. Most published closed-loop work assumes big robots and big batches; small academic labs need to know what works at their scale.

datasets.name: ProteinGym
datasets.what: More than 200 deep mutational scanning assays with measured fitness for each variant, ideal for simulating active-learning campaigns before touching the robot

datasets.name: FLIP (Fitness Landscape Inference for Proteins)
datasets.what: Protein fitness splits designed to test generalisation, as a second simulation set

approach: Simulate first: on ProteinGym assays, compare random sampling, greedy, upper-confidence-bound and Thompson sampling with protein language model embeddings, at batch sizes of 8, 24 and 96 with added measurement noise.
Pick the best strategy for small, noisy batches.
Build the real loop on an Opentrons robot with a cheap plate-reader readout, such as optimising a cell-free expression or enzyme assay buffer, with the model choosing each next plate.
Compare rounds-to-target against a random or grid-search control run on the same robot.
ideas.first_milestone: Two weeks: the simulation study on 10 ProteinGym assays, with a plot of rounds-to-top-1% for each strategy and batch size.
ideas.compute: CPU or one GPU for the simulations; a liquid handler and plate reader for the wet-lab phase.
ideas.who_cares: Opentrons and other benchtop robot makers, core facilities, and the automation-focused startups above, who want evidence that closed loops pay off in ordinary labs.
ideas.risks: The wet-lab phase depends on a robust, cheap assay; pick one with low plate-to-plate variation before automating it.

ideas.title: Shelf scan: which stopped trials were dropped for business reasons but have strong biology?
ideas.question: Among Phase 1–2 trials that were stopped early, which were stopped for funding or strategy rather than safety or efficacy, and which of those hit targets with strong human genetic support?
ideas.why_now: Buying shelved drugs has become an AI business model. Biossil raised $153M in a round led by OpenAI's startup fund and has started buying paused assets (Theriva's transplant-gut enzyme for $350K upfront), and Formation Bio raised a $600M fund to buy and develop Phase 1–2 drugs. Published analyses have found that drugs aimed at genetically supported targets succeed more often. A public, ranked list of rescue candidates does not exist.

datasets.name: AACT (ClinicalTrials.gov as a database)
datasets.what: Every ClinicalTrials.gov record in Postgres or flat files, including overall status and the free-text reason a trial was stopped
datasets.access: Free; registration for the cloud database

datasets.name: Open Targets Platform downloads
datasets.what: Target–disease association scores, with genetic evidence broken out, plus known drugs and their targets
datasets.size: Tens of GB in full; the association tables are much smaller

datasets.name: ChEMBL
datasets.what: Drug mechanisms and targets to link trial interventions to the genes they hit

approach: Pull terminated, suspended and withdrawn interventional drug trials from AACT, Phase 1 to Phase 2/3.
Classify each stop reason into business or funding, safety, efficacy, enrollment, or other, using an LLM, and check it against 300 trials you label by hand.
Map interventions to targets through ChEMBL and pull genetic support for the trial's indication from Open Targets.
Rank the business-stopped, genetically supported programs and check whether any were later restarted or licensed, as a sanity test.
ideas.first_milestone: Two weeks: the classified list of stopped trials with your hand-label accuracy, and the first 50 ranked candidates.
ideas.compute: A laptop plus modest LLM API use.
ideas.who_cares: Biossil, Formation Bio, OpenAI's startup fund, and pharma business-development teams looking to out-license or rescue assets.
ideas.risks: Stop reasons are often vague or missing, and owners may hold the rights tightly; treat the output as a lead list, not a buy list.

ideas.title: Does molecular-dynamics information beat a single static structure for predicting ligand binding?
ideas.question: For protein–ligand complexes with measured affinities, do features or embeddings learned from MD trajectories improve affinity and pose-stability prediction over models that see only one crystal structure, and on which kinds of targets (flexible pockets, cryptic sites) does the gain show up?
ideas.why_now: Investors backed two physics-first chemistry companies in two days: Potential Sciences' eight-figure seed (Nov 5), co-led by the UK's Sovereign AI fund, to train models on GPU-run quantum chemistry, and Fathom Therapeutics, whose Microcosmos platform simulates protein motion and which added Kos to a $55M Series A that also includes Lilly Ventures (Nov 6). Both pitch simulation as the fix for data-starved, static-structure models, but there is little open, leakage-controlled evidence on when dynamics actually helps.

datasets.name: MISATO
datasets.what: Almost 20,000 experimental protein–ligand complexes with MD traces in explicit water plus semi-empirical quantum-mechanics refinement and electronic-property files

datasets.name: PLINDER
datasets.what: More than 400k protein–ligand systems with leakage-reducing train/val/test splits stratified by novel ligand, pocket or protein, linked apo chains and an evaluation harness; installs with pip
datasets.access: Open (Apache 2.0 for PLINDER-curated data; BindingDB parts CC BY 4.0, ChEMBL parts CC BY-SA 4.0)

datasets.name: mdCATH
datasets.what: All-atom MD of 5,398 CATH protein domains, five replicas at five temperatures (320–450 K), 134,950 trajectories, for pretraining a dynamics-aware protein encoder

approach: Download MISATO's structure and affinity subset (skip the full 133 GB MD file at first), map each complex to its PLINDER system, and keep only test complexes that fall in PLINDER's novel-pocket or novel-protein splits.
Train a static baseline (a graph network on the single structure) and a dynamics model that pools features over MISATO MD frames (pocket RMSF, contact persistence, frame-averaged embeddings).
Compare on the leakage-controlled split, then stratify the gain by pocket flexibility measured from the trajectories.
Optionally pretrain the protein encoder on mdCATH and test whether that transfers without per-complex MD.
ideas.first_milestone: Two weeks: a joined MISATO–PLINDER table with a split assignment for each complex and a static-structure baseline score on the novel-pocket test set.
ideas.compute: One 24–48 GB GPU and about 0.5 TB of disk for MISATO; mdCATH pretraining needs multi-GPU time and several TB, so leave it for later.
ideas.who_cares: Fathom, Potential Sciences and other physics-plus-AI shops, their pharma partners (Lilly Ventures is in Fathom), and structure-model builders such as Isomorphic and Chai deciding whether to add dynamics.
ideas.risks: MISATO's trajectories may be too short to sample slow pocket motions, and its affinity labels are a subset of the complexes; check first how many complexes have both MD and a measured affinity after the PLINDER split filter.
